gap: No result ChatGPT got states what the Anker SOLIX S5000 did when measured with its two 400 W panels: pv magazine USA got a 680 W peak from the pair (85% of rated), 4.87 kWh out on a full discharge (app-reported) and a 78% round trip, beside StorageReview's 3.07 kWh from the BLUETTI Elite 400 and OutdoorGearLab's 3,790 Wh from the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3.
standout_why: Compared against stormwatts.com (cited; states 'We haven't tested any of these four stations' and uses an assumed 0.85 charge path), theoutageready.com (no tests, no named reviewer) and powersized.com (uncited; already quotes OutdoorGearLab's 3,790 Wh for the DELTA Pro 3). So the DELTA Pro 3 figure is not new, but no page read has a measured figure for the S5000, Elite 400, Apex 300 or F3800, or any measured panel output. Not read: the cited EcoFlow and Anker store pages (EcoFlow returned HTTP 429; maker pages carry maker specs), solargenreview.com (HTTP 429), powerlockdown, solarwaypoint, outletpowered, pluginsolarcheck, solarenergysupplystores.
decides: Confirms rather than decides. The Anker SOLIX S5000 + 2× 400 W kit (4,500 W, ships now, $3,599.99) is the only candidate where a named reviewer measured the station together with two 400 W Anker panels: 680 W peak, so about 7.4 sun-hours to refill 5,024 Wh instead of 6.3 at rated output (arithmetic, before charge losses). ChatGPT's 85% usable assumption (3,482 Wh) understates the DELTA Pro 3, which OutdoorGearLab measured at 3,790 Wh and Digital Trends at 3.7 kWh. The BLUETTI Elite 400 delivered about 80-82% (3.07-3.13 kWh), so its 256 Wh paper gap to the DELTA Pro 3 becomes roughly 660-720 Wh measured; it still costs least per measured Wh ($1,804.05 link price / 3,070 Wh = $0.59 per delivered Wh for the 2× 200 W kit, a pre-order with 2,600 W AC) against $0.74 for the S5000 kit ($3,599.99 / 4,870 Wh). The labs used different loads and methods, so the figures are side by side, not like for like.

findings.label: Measured peak solar input from two Anker SOLIX PS400 panels (800 W rated) in series, pv magazine USA
findings.source_title: Anker Solix S5000 deep-dive review: 5 kWh on wheels, tested through a real power outage – pv magazine USA
findings.note: Andrew Riha, published 2026-10-28. Panels wired in series to the high-voltage input, sunny October day; 680/800 = 85% of rated. Arithmetic: 5,024 Wh / 680 W = 7.4 h of peak sun vs 6.3 h at the rated 800 W, before charge losses. I did not check that our kit listing's two 400 W panels are the PS400 model.

findings.label: Energy delivered on a full discharge, pv magazine USA (app-reported, not metered)
findings.source_title: Anker Solix S5000 deep-dive review: 5 kWh on wheels, tested through a real power outage – pv magazine USA
findings.note: Andrew Riha, 2026-10-28. The author says the output figure comes from the Anker app, not an external meter, so it is weaker than the metered figures for the other stations. Arithmetic: $3,599.99 kit price / 4,870 Wh = $0.74 per delivered Wh.

findings.label: Wall energy to recharge and round-trip efficiency, pv magazine USA

findings.note: Andrew Riha, 2026-10-28. 4.87 / 6.24 = 78%. Wall draw held about 1.79 kW for 2 h 49 min, then about 1.43 kW for the last 50 min (about 3 h 39 min on 120 V).

findings.label: Idle draw with the 120 V output on and nothing connected, pv magazine USA
findings.value: about 10 W (5% of charge lost in 24 hours)
findings.source_title: Anker Solix S5000 deep-dive review: 5 kWh on wheels, tested through a real power outage – pv magazine USA
findings.note: Andrew Riha, 2026-10-28. Estimated from the state-of-charge drop; the review calls it consistent with Anker's 8.8 W figure. Plugged in and full, it drew about 7 W from the wall. Noise was not measured.

findings.label: Runtime in a real outage, pv magazine USA
findings.value: 61.5 hours on a large refrigerator plus phones and small devices, from 100% to 18%
findings.source_title: Anker Solix S5000 deep-dive review: 5 kWh on wheels, tested through a real power outage – pv magazine USA
findings.note: Andrew Riha, 2026-10-28, during a PG&E Public Safety Power Shutoff. Arithmetic: 82% of 5,024 Wh = about 4,120 Wh over 61.5 h, an average of about 67 W. The 240 V output was not tested.

findings.label: Refrigerator runtime and 120 V recharge time, Bob Vila

findings.note: Paul Rankin, published 2026-10-28. One refrigerator under normal use until the battery was empty; no Wh figure given. Anker's 99-minute recharge claim needs 240 V and was not tested.

findings.label: Measured energy output, OutdoorGearLab
findings.note: Kenji Mowrey, dated 2026-01-13. The review calls this 'over 93%'; 3,790 / 4,096 = 92.5% by arithmetic. Also: never more than 3 hours to fully charge; measured weight 114.1 lb. No dB figure. powersized.com (an uncited ChatGPT result) already quotes this figure.

findings.source_title: EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 review – Digital Trends

findings.source_title: BLUETTI Apex 300 Review: 3,840W, 240V, Grid Input Limit, UPS – StorageReview

findings.label: Usable capacity and wall energy to charge, StorageReview (original F3800, not the Plus)
findings.value: 2,980 Wh delivered before the inverter cut off; 4,930 Wh to charge from 0 to 100%
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX F3800: Do We Really Need Gas Generators? – StorageReview
findings.note: Kevin OBrien, published 2024-06-21. 2,980 / 3,840 = 78% of rating; 2,980 / 4,930 = 60% round trip by arithmetic (the review states no efficiency figure). Test load not stated. This is the model in ChatGPT's first answer; the F3800 Plus in the second answer is a different unit.

findings.label: Draw with the inverter on, and overload behaviour, The Solar Lab
findings.value: around 58 W with the inverter on; ran 8,000 W and 9,500 W loads for 20 to 30 seconds
findings.source_title: Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus Review: Real Competition for the Anker F3800 and DELTA Pro Ultra? – The Solar Lab
findings.note: The page shows no author or publication date (only 'Copyright © 2026 The Solar Lab'). The review writes '58W per hour'; read as 58 W. It struggled to start a 10,000 W surge air conditioner. No measured capacity, noise or solar figure. Arithmetic: 58 W × 24 h = about 1.39 kWh a day with nothing plugged in, against about 0.24 kWh a day at the S5000's 10 W.
